evidence.claim: The first state effort followed a different crossing: work began on a Cascade Pass wagon road in 1897, but floods destroyed most of it.
evidence.quote: The Cascade Pass route began to be roughed out in 1897 and shortly afterward, state highway maps showed the road as either State Highway 1 or the Cascade Wagon Road. In the following years, floods on the Cascade River took out most of the work completed on the road

evidence.claim: Later, development of the Skagit hydroelectric project encouraged highway promoters to pursue Washington Pass.
evidence.quote: The development of the Skagit River Hydroelectric Project spurred boosters to lobby the state for a new route across Washington Pass

evidence.claim: Politicians, lobbyists and business owners formed the North Cascades Highway Association in 1953; the completed highway opened on September 2, 1972.
evidence.quote: In 1953, the North Cascades Highway Association was formed with politicians, lobbyists, and business owners from both sides of the North Cascades taking part.

evidence.claim: the completed highway opened on September 2, 1972.
evidence.quote: The North Cascades Highway officially opened on September 2, 1972

evidence.claim: The highway’s arrival also reshaped Winthrop, which renovated its buildings with Old West false fronts and boardwalk sidewalks to attract the new traffic.
evidence.quote: The Methow Valley town of Winthrop renovated its buildings into an Old West theme with false-front buildings and boardwalk sidewalks in a bid to attract tourists on the new highway.

evidence.claim: Driving east from Sedro-Woolley, follow the Skagit past Concrete and Rockport to Marblemount, then continue through Newhalem to Diablo Lake.
evidence.quote: The highway travels east along the Skagit River, climbing uphill into the Cascade Mountains and passing the towns of Lyman and Concrete, located below Lake Shannon and Baker Lake. At Rockport, SR 20 intersects the eastern terminus of SR 530, which continues towards Darrington and Arlington.

evidence.claim: Driving east from Sedro-Woolley, follow the Skagit past Concrete and Rockport to Marblemount, then continue through Newhalem to Diablo Lake.
evidence.quote: After passing Marblemount, the highway enters North Cascades National Park and Whatcom County. It heads further northeast through Newhalem, a preserved company town for Seattle City Light, and the narrow Diablo Canyon to the Diablo Dam and Diablo Lake

evidence.claim: A long hairpin skirts the lake’s southern arm before the road reaches Ross Lake and climbs toward the passes.
evidence.quote: The roadway makes a long hairpin turn around the southern arm of the lake, crossing it at a narrow point and passing a scenic viewpoint, and continues northeast to Ross Lake. From Ross Lake, SR 20 follows Ruby Creek and Canyon Creek, heading southeast out of the national park and back into Skagit County. The highway crosses Rainy Pass

evidence.claim: Beyond Washington Pass, another hairpin begins the descent toward Mazama, followed by Winthrop and Twisp along the Methow River.
evidence.quote: SR 20 turns north and crosses Washington Pass into Okanogan County, making a hairpin turn and beginning its descent into Eastern Washington.

evidence.claim: Beyond Washington Pass, another hairpin begins the descent toward Mazama, followed by Winthrop and Twisp along the Methow River.
evidence.quote: SR 20 travels northeast along Early Winters Creek and the base of Delancy Ridge towards Mazama, where it meets the Methow River. evidence.claim: Concrete’s name joined two separate cement-making towns on opposite sides of the Baker River.
evidence.quote: In 1905, a settlement across the Baker River came into being due to the building of the Washington Portland Cement Company and was named "Cement City." After the Superior Portland Cement Company plant was built in Baker in 1908, it was decided to merge the two towns.

evidence.claim: Cement City developed with the Washington Portland Cement Company in 1905; Baker gained a Superior Portland Cement Company plant in 1908.
evidence.quote: In 1905, a settlement across the Baker River came into being due to the building of the Washington Portland Cement Company and was named "Cement City." After the Superior Portland Cement Company plant was built in Baker in 1908

evidence.claim: The communities merged as Concrete in 1909.
evidence.quote: Inhabitants of the new community settled on the name "Concrete" and the town was so christened and officially incorporated on May 8, 1909.

evidence.claim: The town sits where the Baker meets the Skagit, and its tall cement silos appear in the film This Boy’s Life.
evidence.quote: The tiny town of Concrete sits at the confluence of the Baker and Skagit rivers. Stroll its quaint streets and enjoy water activities, or visit the towering cement silos, which appear in the film This Boy’s Life .

evidence.claim: The lower Baker River divides the town, which lies mostly on the Skagit’s north bank. Mount Baker stands to the northwest, with Mount Shuksan almost directly north.
evidence.quote: The town lies mostly on the north bank of the Skagit River, and is split into half by the lower Baker River (a tributary to the Skagit River).  Mount Baker, a stratovolcano, lies northwest of Concrete and Mount Shuksan lies almost directly north.

evidence.claim: Look for the tall cement silos that appear in This Boy’s Life.
evidence.quote: visit the towering cement silos, which appear in the film This Boy’s Life

evidence.claim: Diablo Lake’s turquoise water carries finely ground rock from surrounding glaciers, suspended as glacial flour.
evidence.quote: The turquoise hue of the lake's water is attributed to surrounding glaciers grinding rocks into glacial flour that stays suspended in the lake.

evidence.claim: The water itself is held by Diablo Dam, between Ross and Gorge lakes on the Skagit River.
evidence.quote: Created by Diablo Dam, the lake is located between Ross Lake and Gorge Lake on the Skagit River

evidence.claim: Construction finished in 1930, and the dam began operating in 1936 as part of Seattle City Light’s hydroelectric project.
evidence.quote: The Diablo Dam is a part of the Skagit River Hydroelectric Project, which is owned and operated by Seattle City Light. Construction finished in 1930 and the dam became operational in 1936.

evidence.claim: The highway curves around the southern arm, crosses a narrow part of the reservoir and passes a scenic viewpoint.
evidence.quote: The roadway makes a long hairpin turn around the southern arm of the lake, crossing it at a narrow point and passing a scenic viewpoint

evidence.claim: Diablo’s company town was established to house the dam builders. When completed, the 389-foot dam was the tallest in the world.
evidence.quote:
The town of Diablo was established to house the workers building the dam.
The result was a power-generating dam that holds a reservoir known as Diablo Lake. At the time it was completed, Diablo Dam, at 389 feet (119 m), was the tallest dam in the world.

evidence.claim: The lake’s turquoise color comes from glacial flour suspended in the water.
evidence.quote: The turquoise hue of the lake's water is attributed to surrounding glaciers grinding rocks into glacial flour that stays suspended in the lake.
